text:
Verses 180-186

(7:180) To Allah belong the most excellent names, so supplicate Him by them, and abandon those who commit sacrilege in His names.

Soon they shall be requited for what they used to do.

(7:181) Among those We have created are a nation who guide by the truth and do justice thereby.

(7:182) As for those who deny Our signs, We will draw them imperceptibly [into ruin], whence they do not know.

(7:183) And I will grant them respite, for My devising is indeed sure.

(7:184) Have they not reflected that there is no madness in their companion, [and that] he is just a manifest warner?

(7:185) Have they not contemplated the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, and whatever things Allah has created, and that maybe their time has already drawn near? So what discourse will they believe after this?!

(7:186) Whomever Allah leads astray has no guide, and He leaves them bewildered in their rebellion.

Introduction

This section builds on the last section by defining the criterion of guidance and error: it is whether one calls God by His excellent names, or commits sacrilege with respect to His names. All people—whether religious

or atheist, educated or illiterate—acknowledge God through their fiṭrah (primal nature, innate disposition, initial makeup). They know intuitively that this visible world depends on a reality that upholds all its parts and gives order to it. That reality is God, from Whom everything originates, and to Whom everything returns. He is the One Who bestows upon the world any beauty or perfection that it has. All is from Him and belongs to Him. Notwithstanding this essential agreement, people can be classified into three groups with respect to their view of God:

(1) Some people describe God with names that are only befitting of Him. These are names that affirm all perfection for God, and negate all defect and deficiency from Him.

(2) Some people commit sacrilege in His names, meaning that they distort the divine names and ascribe them to other beings. Here are some examples of such people:

(a) Atheists and materialists: they ascribe qualities that are exclusively God’s—such as creating, giving life, and providing sustenance—to nature or matter.

(b) Idol-worshipers: they ascribe good and prosperity to their gods. (c) Some People of the Book, who describe their prophets or saints with divine qualities.

(d) Some believers [that is, Muslims in particular, or monotheists more generally] who treat the means and instruments in the world as independent causes, while the only independent force in the world is God.

(3) Some people believe in God, but they too commit sacrilege in His names through ascribing certain qualities and actions to Him that are not befitting of Him. Here are some examples of such beliefs:

(a) God is physical.

(b) He has a location.

(c) He can be perceived with our senses in certain conditions.

(d) His knowledge, will and power are like our knowledge, will and power.

(e) His existence endures in time.

(f) It is possible for wrong actions or ignorant rulings to issue from Him.

All of these are forms of committing sacrilege with respect to His names.

These three groups can be further generalized into two groups in reality: (i) One group calls God through His excellent names. They worship

Allah, Who is possessor of glory and grace. They are those who are guided to the truth. (ii) Another group commits sacrilege in His name, through either applying His names to other beings, or applying their names to Him. They are straying, and their path leads to hell, although they are at different levels and degrees of error.

God further clarifies that all guidance is from Him. Guidance is a positive quality, and its reality belongs to God. Meanwhile, it is not possible to attribute ḍalāl (misguidance, straying, error) to God whatsoever.

The reality of ḍalāl is lacking God’s guidance, which makes it a privative and non-existential quality. Yet, sometimes it is used as a quality that the person “possesses” or an inseparable trait of a soul. W hat is meant in these cases is being deprived and cut offfrom God’s blessing. This is itself a divine punishment for those who choose error over guidance. It is how God penalizes those who reject His signs and communications. It is in this sense that the Qur’an attributes ḍalāl to God. His role here is to give them respite (imlāʾ) and lead them step-by-step into temptation (istidrāj). The previous set of verses said that guidance and error are all from God [7:178]. These verses elaborate on the essence and reality of that. They clarify that one’s guidance depends on calling God by His excellent names—and all excellent names belong to God—while one’s error

is a result of committing sacrilege in His names. A group of people are guided by God’s guidance, such that they do not deviate from Him to others. And a group of people stray, deviate from His names, and deny His

signs. God drives the second group to hell because of denying His signs and communications, as He said: Certainly We have created for hell many of the jinn and humans… (7:179). He does this through a gradual process of leaving them on their own and giving them respite.

Commentary

(7:180) To Allah belong the most excellent names (al-asmāʾ al-ḥusná), so supplicate Him by them, and abandon those who commit sacrilege in His names. Soon they shall be requited for what they used to do.

Linguistically speaking, the word ism (name, noun) is something that serves to denote and indicate something. This can be in two ways: (1) Sometimes it is a word that indicates a certain meaning, such as nonproper nouns. (2) Sometimes it is a proper noun that refers to a certain

being, such as Zayd and ʿAmr. The latter is especially true about improvised proper nouns [which are unprecedented by any particular meaning].

The word al-ḥusná is the feminine form of aḥsan (best, most beautiful, most excellent). This shows that what is meant by “names” here is not merely proper names, but names that indicate a meaning and describe the qualities of the being. In fact, one may question whether any of God’s names is purely a proper name. Furthermore, the verse is not merely about meaningful and descriptive names, but names that have an element of ḥusn (goodness, beauty, excellence); and not just that, but the highest degree of ḥusn when compared to other names with respect to God.

For instance, “courageous” and “self-restrained” are good qualities, but they are not applicable to God’s sanctity since they imply an integral element of physicality that cannot be stripped from them. If such elements

[of deficiency and materiality] can be divested of a name, then it can be applied to God, such as al-Jawād (the Generous), al-ʿAdl (the All-Just) and al-Raḥīm (the Ever-Merciful).

Therefore, an “excellent name” of God would be a name that has two properties: (1) It denotes a quality of perfection. (2) It is free from all defect, and unmixed with any non-existential aspect, unless it can be divested and abstracted from that aspect. The second condition refers to anything that implies some need or deficiency on the part of God, such as being physical, having physical properties,1 committing evil, being unjust or having a lack.

It should be noted that all divine names are still part of our language.

1 For the difference between being physical and having physical properties, see my first footnote on the section titled “What is Meant by Seeing” above, under verses 7:138-154. (Trans.)

They are words that we have designed for human applications, which always have an element of limitation, need and imperfection. However, even though all these names and qualities originate from the limited world of human existence, they can be classified into two types: (1) There are some concepts that are inherently limited, such that we cannot negate their element of need and deficiency. Some examples are body, color and size. (2) There are other concepts that can be divested from human limitations, such as knowledge, power and life. In the case of human knowledge, we develop a mental image of something from the outside world through our physical senses. Our knowledge is to conceptually encompass that mental image. Human power is the capacity to act through the physical movement of our muscles. Human life is our state of having knowledge and power through the means and instruments of each. None of these qualities is befitting of God, but we can strip their material aspects from their core meanings. Then knowledge would be encompassing something through the presence of that thing before the knower. Power would be the capacity to give existence to something. And life would be the quality of having knowledge and power.1 These abstracted meanings can be safely applied to God, since they are free from the human aspects of limitation and need. Based on both rational proof and scriptural evidence, all qualities of perfection belong to God. He is the One Who bestows2 these qualities upon other beings without any previous model or example to follow.

Hence, God is Knowledgeable, Powerful, and Living. He does not possess these attributes in the way that we do, but in a way that is appropriate to His precinct of sanctity, which means the reality and essence of these perfections, without any element of imperfection.

The verse literally says, “Belong to God the most excellent names,” where the predicate (Belong to God) precedes the subject (the most excellent names). This way of expression indicates exclusivity. Al-asmāʾ is a

plural noun (asmāʾ) used with the article al-. Such usage shows universality and encompassment. This means that all beautiful names in existence

belong to God alone, and no one else has any part in them. Nevertheless,

1 Knowledge and power can also be interpreted as consciousness and force, respectively. (Trans.)

2 “Bestows” can be interpreted as “manifests” for more mystical and metaphysical accuracy. (Trans.)

we see [in the Qur’an] that God sometimes describes others with these qualities—such as knowledge, life, creation and mercy. Therefore, what is meant here is that the reality of these qualities exclusively belongs to Him. This is confirmed by the apparent meaning—or rather, by the explicit text—of many verses, such as: that power, altogether, belongs to Allah

(2:165); all honor belongs to Allah (4:139); they do not comprehend anything of His knowledge except what He wills (2:255); He is the Living One,

there is no god except Him (40:65). These verses show that the reality of any quality of excellence and perfection belongs to God alone. No other being has any share of these qualities except to the extent and in the way that He bestows upon them according to His will.

The same can be inferred from other verses that talk about God’s names in plural: Allah—there is no god except Him—to Him belong the most excellent names (20:8); Say: Invoke “Allah” or invoke “the All-Merciful.” Whichever [of His Names] you may invoke, to Him belong the most excellent names (17:110); To Him belong the most excellent names. Whatever there is in the heavens glorifies Him and [whatever there is in] the earth (59:24). The apparent meaning of all these verses is that the reality of any beautiful name belongs to God alone.

Some exegetes have suggested that the article al- in al-asmāʾ [“the” in the most excellent names] is a definite article.1 However, this is an unwarranted interpretation, and there is no evidence for it in the verses. This

interpretation stems from certain narrations which enumerate the most excellent names of God. We shall discuss them in our next examination of the narrations, by God’s will.

… so supplicate Him (fa-udʿūhu, from daʿwah) by them…: The word daʿwah can have three meanings: (1) Naming. When someone is given a certain name or title, it is said: daʿawtuhu Zaydan or daʿawtuka ʿAbdAllāh.2 (2) Calling. The meaning would be: Call God by these names like O All-Merciful, O Ever-Merciful. (3) Worshiping. The meaning would be: Worship God while you admit that He possesses these excellent qualities and beautiful meanings.

1 In other words, the verse is not saying that “all excellent names belong to God,” but it is saying that “certain excellent names which are already known to the audience belong to Him.” (Trans.)

2 The meaning would be: “Use these excellent names to refer to God.” (Trans.) Exegetes have offered all of the above three interpretations, but the usage of duʿāʾ in other similar contexts in the Qur’an favors the last. Here are a few examples:

(i) A verse that we already quoted above: Say: Invoke (udʿū) “Allah” or invoke “the All-Merciful.” Whichever [of His Names] you may invoke, to Him belong the most excellent names (17:110).

(ii) Your Lord has said, “Call Me (udʿūnī), and I will answer you!” Indeed those who are disdainful of My worship (ʿibādatī) will enter hell in utter disgrace (40:60). In this verse, the words duʿāʾ (call) and ʿibādah (worship, service) are used interchangeably.

(iii) Another similar substitution is found in these verses: W ho is more astray than him who invokes (yadʿū) besides Allah such as would not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, and who are oblivious of their invocation (duʿāʾihim)?When humankind are mustered [on the Day of Judgement] they will be their enemies, and they will disavow their worship (ʿibādatihim) (46:5-6).

(iv) He is the Living One, there is no god except Him. So supplicate Him (fa-udʿūhu), putting exclusive faith in Him (40:65). What is meant here is exclusive worship (ʿibādah) of God.

The above interpretation is also confirmed by the subsequent part of this very verse: and abandon those who commit sacrilege in His names. Soon they shall be requited for what they used to do (7:180). The verse talks about being requited for their actions. If the intended meaning of supplicate Him by them was that “you should give these names to God” or “you should call Him with these names” then the verse should have ended by referring to their speech and descriptions—much like the verse: Soon He will requite them for their descriptions (waṣfahum) (6:139)—not by referring to their actions. Nevertheless, naming and calling are also implications of worship. The meaning is: “All names that are the best of names belong to God. So worship Him and turn to Him through these names.” God knows best. … and abandon those who commit sacrilege (yulʿidūna) in His names…: The word in the verse can be recited as either yalḥadūna, derived from laḥd; or as yulḥidūna, derived from ilḥād (following the transitive verbal pattern ifʿāl). The two are synonymous. Both laḥd and ilḥād mean “inclining from the middle to one side.” Laḥad is a part of a grave that is on one side, as opposed to ḍarīḥ, which is in the middle. It is narrated from some lexicographers that laḥd means “inclining to one side,” while ilḥād means “dispute, quarrel.”

… Soon they shall be requited for what they used to do: This part of the verse is not connected to the previous part with a conjunction [like and, or, then, so, because]. The reason for this is that the sentence serves to answer an implied question (called a prolepsis). W hen the verse says: abandon those who commit sacrilege in His names, one would naturally ask, “What will happen to them?” The verse explains: Soon they shall be requited for what they used to do.

There is more to discuss on the topic of God’s most excellent names, which we shall continue after we finish the exposition of this set of verses, by God’s will.

(7:181) Among those We have created are a nation who guide by the truth and do justice thereby.

We discussed some of the points relating to this verse under a similar verse above: Among the people of Moses is a nation who guide [the people] by the truth and do justice thereby (7:159). The current verse is in a set of verses that divide all humankind into either guided or misguided. Based on the previous verse, the criterion for this division is whether one calls God through the best names that befit Him, or one commits sacrilege with respect to His names. The verse is saying that humankind consists of some group—either small or large—that are truly guided.

What is intended here is genuine guidance and misguidance, which are attributable to God’s doing: Whomever Allah guides is rightly guided (al-muhtadī), and whomever He leads astray—it is they who are the losers

(7:178). Muhtadī is derived from ihtidāʾ (being guided, receiving guidance). If one is truly guided (muhtadī), it shows that the person has received genuine guidance (hidāyah), which can only come from God as its sole possessor.

God’s act of guidance does not fail or miss its objective in any way. It secures one from error and straying. We discussed this under other verses such as: So if these disbelieve in them, We have certainly entrusted them to a people who will never disbelieve in them (6:89). Furthermore, one who guides to the truth cannot receive guidance from anyone other than God. This is inferred from the verse: Is He who guides to the truth worthier to be followed, or he who guides not unless he is [himself] guided? (10:35). The reader should reflect on this.

Given the above explanations, the ascription of guidance to the nation mentioned in this verse shows that they are immune from error and fault through clinging and subscribing to God. This can be interpreted in two ways: (1) The entire nation in this verse has this infallibility, which means that the verse is specifically about the prophets and saints. (2) The verse uses the quality of some members of a group to describe the whole. There are other examples of this usage in the Qur’an: Certainly We gave the Children of Israel the Book, judgement and prophethood (45:16); He [God] made you [O Children of Israel] kings (5:20); that you may be witnesses to the people (2:143). In these verses, only a subset of the audience

is characterized by the qualities described in the verse. God knows best. The meaning is: We do not expect from you something that is unfeasible and beyond human capability, because among those We have created are a nation who are genuinely covered with divine guidance, and

who guide to the truth. This is because God has blessed them with His particular guidance.

(7:182) As for those who deny Our signs, We will draw them imperceptibly [into ruin] (sa-nastadrijuhum, from istidrāj), whence they do

not know.

Istidrāj is “to raise or lower something or someone step by step.” It is to gradually approach something or some place. Given the verse’s context, what is meant here is to approach ruin and destruction, either in this

world or in the hereafter.

… whence they do not know: This qualification means that they do not see, feel, or realize their gradual damnation. This is because they are completely engrossed in the apparent glamor, pleasures and occupations of the material life.

There are two possible interpretations for istidrāj (gradual ruin) in this verse:

(1) They constantly get closer to their own destruction through adding to their wrongdoing, but they do not pause to reflect on their grim end since God keeps renewing and perpetuating His material bounties upon them. We discussed this idea under the verses: Then We changed the evil for good until they multiplied [in numbers] (7:95); Never be misled by the bustle of the faithless in the towns. It is a trivial enjoyment; then their refuge

is hell, and it is an evil resting place (3:196-197).1 (2) Those who deny the signs and communications of God cut off themselves from the remembrance of their Lord. They cling to the apparent means and instruments in order to secure themselves. As a result, they

lose inner peace and the composure of the heart. This is their punishment; they are afflicted by inner agitation, anxiety and stress. The means and sources that they hope in will fail them, and difficulties will pile up on them. They think that this is what life is all about, not realizing the true meaning of a blissful life. Hence they fall into a vicious cycle: they continue seeking and accumulating the adornments of this world, and see that as an extension and increase of blessings upon them. But that only adds to their punishment, until they eventually land on eternal punishment in the hereafter, which will be most calamitous and bitter (54:46). This is how they are on a slippery slope toward punishment from when they deny the signs and communications of their Lord, until they encounter their day, which they are promised (43:83, 70:42).

The second interpretation can be matched with these verses: Lo! The hearts find rest in Allah’s remembrance (13:28); But whoever disregards My remembrance, he shall have a tight life (20:124); So let not their wealth and children impress you: Allah only desires to punish them with these in the life of this world, and that their souls may depart while they are faithless (9:55). However, this sense of istidrāj is not compatible with the next

verse: And I will grant them respite (7:183). Hence, we must go with the first interpretation.

(7:183) And I will grant them respite (umlī, from imlā.), for My devising is indeed sure.

Imlāʾ is synonymous with imhāl (to postpone, to delay, to extend). This verse involves a shifiiofiaddress from the first person plural to the first person singular. There are two explanations for this shif : (1) It shows extra emphasis on their deprivation of divine mercy, and their leading

1 See volume 7 (1st ed.), p. 131 of the English translation, and the very first part

of the current volume. (Trans.)

into damnation.1 (2) The verse is about postponing their judgment and punishment until their appointed time. This is more elaborately stated in the verse: were it not for a prior decree of your Lord [granting them reprieve] until a specified time, decision would have been made between them (42:14). That is what God said to Adam upon his fall on the earth: On the earth shall be your abode and sustenance for a time (2:36). This is a decree of God’s that is attributable to Him alone. That is why it is expressed in the first person singular. However, in the case of istidrāj, which means bestowing and renewing blessings one after another upon the servant, God’s angels are also involved as intermediaries. That is why the last verse was in the first person plural.

… for My devising is indeed sure: This sentence explains and justifies both the last verse and the current one. This part is also in the first person singular because it encompasses both istidrāj (gradual ruin through

blessings) and imhāl (giving respite).

(7:184) Have they not reflected that there is no madness (jinnah) in their companion, [and that] he is just a manifest warner?

There is much disagreement among the exegetes about the composition of this verse. The most apparent and direct meaning that springs to

the mind, given the context, is that the verse consists of two complete sentences: (1) Have they not reflected? This is a rhetorical question which implies a negation and rebuke. (2) There is no madness in their companion. This is a confirmation of the Prophet’s claim to prophethood. Meanwhile, the second sentence also clarifies what the audience should reflect upon. The verse can be elaborated as follows: Have they not reflect on the fact that their companion is not a madman—so that this fact would become clear to them? Indeed, there is no madness in him, for he is only a manifest warner.

By referring to the prophet as their companion (ṣāḥib), the verse gives them direction on how to reflect. It is pointing out that the Prophet was among them and in their company throughout his life. So if there were any madness in him, they would have surely known by now. This proves

1 It is as though the speaker (God) is personally taking charge of this affair. (Trans.)

that the news that he has brought is a message of warning, not a symptom of madness.

It is said that jinnah is a specific kind of madness. Another possibility is that it means a person of the jinn. This is based on a common belief at the time that madness is when one of the jinn enters the person and talks using the madman’s tongue.

(7:185) Have they not contemplated the kingdom (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth, and whatever things Allah has created, and that maybe their time has already drawn near? So what discourse will they believe after this?!

As we discussed previously, malakūt in the Qur’an refers to the inner aspect of things, through which they face and connect to their Lord. This is deduced from these verses: All His command, when He wills something, is to say to it “Be,” and it is. So glory be to Him in Whose hand is the kingdom (malakūt) of all things (36:82-83). Moreover, observing this divine aspect of things is a necessary concomitant of yaqīn (certitude, conviction). This is inferred from the verse: Thus did We show Abraham the kingdom (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth, that he might be of those who possess certitude (6:75).1

The verse reprimands the audience for neglecting and turning away from the divine aspect of things. Why are they oblivious of this aspect? Why do they not look into it, so that it may realize that the Prophet is calling them to the truth?

… and whatever things Allah has created…: The conjunction “and”

joins this phrase to the heavens in the previous part. The verse literally says, “And what God has created of anything,” where “of anything” (min shayʾ) describes and clarifies “what” (mā).

The meaning is: Why do they not reflect on the creation of the heavens,

1 See volume 1 (1st ed.), p. 191, under verse 2:29; volume 2 (1st ed.), pp. 80-81,

under verse 2:124; and volume 13 (1st ed.), pp. 217ff, under verse 6:75, of the English translation. Also, see verses 7:172-174 above, just before the section titled “Back to the Verse.” (Trans.)

the earth, and anything else that God has created? Not in the sense that they are particular objects—which only leads one to a scientific knowledge of their physical properties—but in the sense that they are dependent beings, that they are connected to another source, that they are in need of a Lord Who directs their affairs and the affairs of all things. That is the Lord of the worlds.

… and that maybe their time has already drawn near…: The verse literally says, “And the possible closing on them of their time,” which is treated as a singular noun.1 That is why the conjunction “and” is used to add this entire phrase [as a single item] to kingdom in the previous part of the verse.

The implied meaning is: “Do they not contemplate on the fact that their death might have drawn near?” Taking this possibility into account could awaken them and help them stop continuously straying in error. Indeed, the forgetting of death is the primary motive that diverts people’s attention from building their eternal life and makes them fall prey to the illusions of this world. Death is a reality that one does not know when it shall occur. If one only realizes that they have no idea about their time of death, and that it could be any time, then that would uproot their inadvertence, and would prevent them from following their desires and prolonging their hopes.

… So what discourse will they believe after this?!: This means that it is rather hopeless that they would believe. Given the context, the demonstrative pronoun “this” refers to the Qur’an. God has manifested Himself to

the people through His speech—the Qur’an—which comprises of rational arguments and moral admonitions that stand to reason. At the same

time, the Qur’an is also a clear miracle. Now, if they do not believe in the religion despite the Qur’an, they will not believe by any other means. As God says elsewhere, He has sealed their hearts, so they do not understand the message of guidance, and do not believe in the truth. Thus He says in the next verse: Whomever Allah leads astray has no guide (7:186).

(7:186) Whomever Allah leads astray has no guide, and He leaves

1 The Arabic particle an (that) in an yakūna is called an maṣdariyyah. It serves to turn the verb that follows it into a maṣdar (gerund, infinitive noun). (Trans.)

them bewildered (yaʿmaʿūna, from ʿamah) in their rebellion.

There are two possible meanings for ʿamah: (1) wandering in error; (2) lack of understanding. The complement of this verse is: “Whomever God guides, no one can mislead.” This is not mentioned here because the verse serves as an explanation and justification for the last verse: So what discourse will they believe…? (7:185). It is as though one has asked, “Why is it that they do not believe?” and this verse explains: “Because whomever Allah leads astray…”

Discussion on the Excellent Names of God 1. What is Meant by the Divine Names and How Can We Know Them?

When we open our eyes, the first thing we get to know is ourselves and the closest things to us. We realize our relation to the outside world based on our need for survival. We notice our organs, faculties and functions that revolve around this need. Those are the first elements of our

knowledge. It does not take long for us to find ourselves as needy beings that do not sustain themselves. And so are our faculties and functions. “Need” is one of the first things that we observe in ourselves, as well as in all other things, including our faculties, our functions, and the outside world. Thus we intuitively arrive at a source that fulfills our needs and removes our deficiency. That is God, Who is the end point of all needs and relations. This primary observation and inference of ours is confirmed by the verse: O humankind! You are the ones who stand in need of Allah, and Allah— He is the Ever-Sufficient (35:15).

History is incapable of pinpointing the origin of the human belief in a deity. As one traces humankind to the most ancient people, one continues to find the belief in some supernatural forces that they subscribed

to. For instance, such beliefs have been discovered in the aboriginals of the Americas and Australia who lead primitive lives in simple communities. They all believe in some deity, although some might have gone astray

with the exact application of this belief. This shows that the belief in some origin—from whom all things emanate—is a necessary requirement of the human fiṭrah (original intuition, primal nature, initial makeup). If one does not arrive at it this, it shows a deviation from one’s fiṭrah. That is like one who accustoms themselfito a toxic substance: their physical nature opposes that at first, but they persist until the substance becomes enjoyable to them.

One of the most basic principles of theology is that the existence of all things traces to God. This means that God possesses everything; otherwise, He would not be able to bestow and confer it on others. Nevertheless,

the reality of certain things is a sense of need; they indicate an element of imperfection. God, however, is free from all need and imperfection, because He is the Source Whom all beings depend on to fulfill their need and complete their imperfection. This clarifies that God is the absolute holder of all mulk (kingdom, sovereignty) and milk (ownership, possession). To Him belongs any quality of perfection that we find in existence,

such as life, power, knowledge, hearing, sight, sustenance, mercy, might, and so on.

This is how we can arrive at the names and attributes of God. For instance:

(i) He is Ever-Living, Omnipotent, Omniscient, Ever-Hearing and Ever-Seeing, because otherwise He would be imperfect. But He is clear of all imperfection.

(ii) He is the Sustainer, the Ever-Merciful, the Ever-Mighty, the LifeGiver, the Death-Giver, the Originator, the Returner and the Resurrector. These are His attributes of action. He possesses these qualities because these acts—giving sustenance, showing mercy, being mighty, giving life, giving death, originating, returning and resurrecting—are His acts.

(iii) He is the All-Glorious, the All-Sacred, the Ever-Sublime, the EverGreat and the Supreme. These names serve to negate from Him all non-existential traits and anything that indicates some deficiency. The above is how we can prove the divine names and attributes in a straightforward way. The Qur’an confirms this through attributing mulk (kingdom, sovereignty) and milk (ownership, possession) to God in their absolute sense. There are numerous verses to this effect, which we do not need to quote here.

2. Defining the Divine Names and Attributes There are some aspects of lack that we find in various parts of the world, such as death, deficiency, poverty, abasement, impotence, ignorance, and so on. As we clarified in the last part, we negate these qualities

of imperfection from God. Now we should add that the negation of some imperfection reduces to the affirmation of its opposite perfection. For instance, negating poverty means affirming richness; negating dishonor means affirming honor; negating weakness means affirming power; and negating ignorance means affirming knowledge.

We also said that we attribute qualities of perfection to God, such as life, power and knowledge. This is because all perfections in existence emanate from Him. Meanwhile, sometimes there are some aspects of def ciency and imperfection that accompany certain qualities of perfection

in some of their instances and applications. We should also negate these aspects from God. For example, consider knowledge. Our knowledge is to conceptually encompass a mental image of an object that we obtain from the outside world through our physical senses. There are some elements of this process that do not befit God, such as the prior existence of

the object in the outside, the intermediation of a mental image, and the need of physical organs and senses. These are due to some deficiency in our existence, while God is free from that. What is applicable to Him is the essence and reality of knowledge, which is to encompass something through the presence of that thing. In short, whenever there is an instance of a positive quality, we should affirm for God its core, which is an existential perfection; and we should negate from Him the aspects that boil

down to some need or imperfection.

There remains another imperfection that we must negate from God:

being limited and defined. If something is limited in any aspect of its existence, it means that there is some greater being that has defined and confined it from outside, for something cannot limit itself. Hence, we also negate all limits and boundaries from God. This means that God is not limited by anything, whether in His essence or in His qualities. That is what He says in the Qur’an: He is the One, the All-Dominant (13:16). This means that His oneness is such oneness that dominates everything. So He is the Being that encompasses all other beings, but Himself is not encompassed by any boundary.

Based on this negation of limits, we arrive at another conclusion: The divine attributes are identical with one another, and they are all identical with the divine essence. They differ only conceptually, but they all refer to the same external reality. If His knowledge, for instance, were different from His power, or if any of His attributes were different from His

essence—as is the case in us humans—then that would mean that His attributes and His essence restrict one another. Then one would be limited, and the other would be its limitation; one would be bounded, and the

other would be its boundary. This would mean that the divine essence is composed, and needs some boundaries to define it. However, God is free from having components and limits. This is the quality of divine oneness (aḥadiyyah), which does not accept any division whatsoever, and does not take on any external or mental multiplicity.

Some scholars favor an apophatic theology, which says:

All divine attributes should be interpreted as negations, because we must clear Him of the qualities of His creation. Hence, when we say that God has knowledge, power and life, what is meant is that He is free from ignorance, impotence and death. The same goes with the other divine attributes.

Our explanations above should clarify the problem with this view.

This view necessitates a negation of all qualities of perfection from God, which is against both our intuitive understanding, and the apparent text of the Qur’an. There are also other similarly implausible views in this regard, such as:

(i) The divine attributes are additional and external to the divine essence.

(ii) We should negate all attributes from God, and only affirm the impacts and effects of those attributes for Him.

All such views are contrary to our intuitive understanding. A more elaborate discussion of them is beyond the scope of the current work. 3. The Classifications of the Divine Names and Attributes a) Affirmative and Negational Attributes As we said above, through our intuitive quest, we arrive at certain attributes of God that have an affirmative nature, such as life and knowledge. These attributes denote divine perfections. He also has some negational attributes, such as al-Quddūs (the All-Sacred) and al-Subbūḥ (the

All-Glorified). These attributes denote tanzīh (incomparability, transcendence). Hence, the divine attributes can be classified in two categories:

thubūtiyyah (affirmative, positive) and salbiyyah (negational, negative, apophatic).

b) Attributes of Essence and Attribute of Action The divine attributes can also be classified as attributes of essence, and attributes of action. The former are qualities that are identical with the divine essence, such as life, power and essential knowledge. The latter are qualities that are additional and external to the divine essence, such as creation and sustenance. The divine essence takes precedence to them in existence. These qualities are extracted and derived from divine actions. Here is an example to illustrate what is meant by derivation here: Consider all the bounties and blessings that we have and enjoy. They can be compared to rations that a king allots to his soldiers. We call these blessings “sustenance” (rizq), and we call God “the Sustainer” (al-Rāziq). The

same can be said about other qualities of action, such as creation, mercy and forgiveness. These qualities are applied to God, and we derive names for Him based on them, but their meanings are not found in Him in the same way that His essential attributes are found in Him, such as life and power. If the divine essence were really characterized by these qualities, then they would also be attributes of essence, not something external to God’s essence. In short, the divine attributes can also be classified as either attributes of essence or attributes of action.

c) Non-Relational, Relational, and Purely Relational Attributes Some of God’s attributes have an independent reality of their own, without being tied to anything outside the divine essence, such as life. These are called nafsiyyah (independent, absolute, non-relational). They do not bear some relation to anything outside the divine essence. There are other attributes which also denote an independent quality, but that quality is relational, such as creation (khalq) and fashioning (ṣunʿ). These are called dhāt iḍāfah (with relation). Finally, there are some attributes that denote a purely relational meaning, such as creatorship (khāliqiyyah) and sustainership (rāziqiyyah). These are called iḍāf yyah maḥḍah (purely relational).1

There are some divine names that are only used for God, as it is said about Allāh and al-Raḥmān. Allāh denotes God as a proper noun, not through its lexical meaning. Al-Raḥmān is among the most excellent names of God, in the sense that its meaning [of mercy] is also found among God’s creatures, as we discussed above.1 This is what we can say within the scope of tafsīr (exposition, commentary) of the Qur’an. There is also a legal discussion here, which is beyond the scope of this book. 4. The Relation of the Divine Names and Attributes to Us and to Themselves

There is no real difference between a ṣifah (attribute, quality) and an ism (name). Their distinction is in terms of what they primarily denote. In the case of an attribute, what comes first is a meaning or quality that is found in some essence, whether that is a separable or inseparable aspect of the essence. In the case of a name, what comes first is the essence itself, although it is viewed in the sense that it bears a certain quality. Therefore, “life” and “knowledge” are attributes, while “living” and “knowledgeable” are names. The function of a word is to denote and indicate a meaning. This means that the reality of an attribute is not its letters, but the meaning that the letters indicate. Similarly, the reality of a name is the meaning

indicated by that word. For instance, the reality of God’s quality of life is not the word “life” but the meaning that corresponds to them. In this case, that reality is the very essence of God, which is identical with divine life. Hence, the words “life” and “living” are both only “names”2 that denote their corresponding meanings. The actual attributes and names of God are not the letters and sounds, but the reality and meaning indicated by them. We said above that, following our intuitive approach, we discover the divine names through observing certain qualities of perfection in existence. From this we can know that God certainly has these qualities, because He is the One Who bestows them upon us. Similarly, by observing (Trans.)

That is how He fulfills our needs and removes our imperfections. For example, when we observe knowledge and power in the world of existence, we ascertain that God possesses knowledge and power, through which He bestows these qualities upon His creation. Similarly, when we observe ignorance and impotence, we deduce that He is free from them, but is characterized by their opposites, which would be knowledge and power. Through them He removes our need of knowledge and impotence. The same analysis can be applied to the other divine attributes.

From this we can deduce an important realization: It is through the divine attributes that God’s creation connects to Him and receives various aspects of existence. In other words, the divine attributes are intermediaries between the divine essence and His creation. If we have knowledge,

power, sustenance and comfort, we receive them from God in the sense that He is Knowledgeable, Powerful, Sustainer and Comforter. Similarly, it is His knowledge that removes our ignorance; it is His power that removes our impotence; it is His glory that removes our abasement; it is His richness that removes our poverty; and it is His forgiveness that removes our

sins. From another angle, we can say that He dominates us through His dominion; He limits us through His limitlessness; He binds us through His boundlessness; He lowers us through His highness; He humbles us through His honor; He rules over us as He wills through His sovereignty; and He manipulates us as He wills through His possession. The reader should reflect on this.

What we just said is in line with how we behave intuitively, according to our fiṭrah (primal nature, innate disposition, initial makeup). For

instance, when one wants riches from God, they do not say, “O DeathGiver! O Humiliator! Make me solvent!” Instead, they call God by relevant names like the Ever-Rich, the Ever-Mighty and the Powerful. Similarly, a sick person who wants to pray for their wellness would say, “O Healer! O Recoverer! O Ever-Kind! O Ever-Merciful! Show me mercy and heal me!” The person would not say, “Heal me, O Vengeful!” The same can be said and observed about the other divine attributes.

The Noble Qur’an also confirms our intuitive understanding and practice, and this is the best evidence for to the truth of the above theory of

God’s names. We see that the verses of the Qur’an end with names that match the content of that verse. Whenever the Qur’an makes a statement, it justifies and backs it by mentioning one or two of God’s name at the end, in accordance to the context. Among all revealed scriptures that we have, the Qur’an is the only book that uses the divine names to establish its claims. Thus it teaches us about the names of God.

We connect to God through His names, and to His names through their effects in our world. The signs of His beauty and majesty link us to His names of beauty and majesty, such as life, knowledge, power, might, magnificence and grandeur. And these names in turn link us to the holy divine essence, on which the entire world of existence depends.

The effects of God’s names differ in terms of breadth and scope. In this sense, they correspond to their concepts, some of which are more inclusive than others. For instance, our qualities of hearing, sight, imagination and intellection are branches of our knowledge [which is their

parent quality]. Then our knowledge, together with power, life and other qualities, is classified under God’s sustenance, bestowment, blessing and benevolence. And these qualities, together with pardon, forgiveness and other qualities, fall under the universal mercy of God.

This shows that the divine names differ in terms of inclusion, restriction, universality and specificity, in accordance to their effects in our world.

Some of these effects are more general, while others are more specific. Their degrees of generality and specificity stem from the realities that they indicate. Our concepts of these qualities would reveal how their underlying realities relate to one another in terms of breadth and inclusion. For example, divine knowledge is more specific compared to divine

life, but it is more general compared to divine hearing, seeing, witnessing, subtlety and awareness. Similarly, “the Sustainer” is a more specific name compared to “the All-Merciful,” but it is more general compared to “the Healer,” “the Helper” and “the Guide.” The same set of relations can be sketched among other names.

The excellent names of God have a wide spectrum that extends vertically. At the bottom of the spectrum, there is one or few names that are

most specific and restricted, such that no other name can be classified under them. Then as we go up, the names become broader and more inclusive. Each name falls under another name that is more encompassing and

universal, until they reach the highest name, which alone embraces the realities of all names. A diverse range of realities come under it together. That is what is often called the Greatest Name (al-ism al-aʿẓam).

It should be clear that the more extensive a name is, the greater, more perfect and more powerful will be the effects and blessings that descend from it upon the world. This is based on the fact that the divine names are intermediaries for any effect or event in existence. That is why the universality and particularity of each name is matched by the universality and particularity of its effect. For the same reason, all effects go back

to the Greatest Name, and all affairs are subject to it.

5. The Greatest Name of God (al-Ism al-Aʿẓam)

It is widely believed that the Greatest Name is a word, just like the other common names of God. It is also believed that if one calls God by this name, their wish will come true. The Greatest Name is believed to be a magical formula that does not fall short of bringing about anything. However, since people have not found this quality in any of the common names of God, including Allah, they have come to the conclusion

that the Greatest Name must have a unique composition of letters that is unknown to us. Otherwise, if we were to discover it, everything would be subservient to our will.

The experts on miraculous prayers and spells believe that the Greatest Name is composed of letters, but not like regular words that are assigned conventionally. Rather, there is an intrinsic connection between the letters and the power of the name. Moreover, the letters and their composition differ according to one’s need and wish. They have their special ways of extrapolating the letters first, and then combining them to make up the desired word in each case. One should refer to their discipline for these ways.1

There are some narrations which may seem to confirm the above view—that the Greatest Name is a word which is made up of letters. For instance, there are narrations that say:

(1) “In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Ever-Merciful” (bism Allāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm) is closer to the Greatest Name of God than the white part of the eye is to the black part.

(2) The Greatest Name is to be found in verse 2:255 (Āyat al-Kursī)

(3) The letters of the Greatest Name are dispersed in Chapter 1 (al-Ḥamd). The Imams know them. Whenever they want, they can assemble them and call God by them, whereby their wish will be granted.

However, an adequate analysis of causality and its properties would make clear that the above notion cannot be correct [in its unrefined, apparent and literal sense]. The law of causality tells us the following principles:

(i) What has real impact in the universe is the existence of a thing [not the verbal utterance of a word that designates something conventionally].

(ii) Every cause has as much power as the degree of its existence. (iii) There must be a real existential concordance between every effect and its cause.

Based on these principles, the Greatest Name cannot be merely a set of letters and sounds that are uttered, for letters and sounds are forms of qualities, which are a sub-category of accidents.1 Nor can it be the meaning indicated by some letters, because a meaning is a mental image, and mental images cannot have a causal effect in the external world, inasmuch as they are mental entities. It is impossible that a sound which we create through our vocal cords—or a concept that we imagine in our minds—would be at such a high plane of existence that we can use it to influence and rule over everything as we wish. That sound or mental image is itself subject to our volition, and is created by us. So how could it be a causal agent in

We should remember that the only reality that acts as a cause in the world is God. So when we say the divine names—and especially the Greatest Name—effect changes in the universe and act as channels for God’s effusions in our world, it means that they act through their realities. And the reality of each name is God Himself, viewed in the light of

a specific attribute that corresponds to that name. Otherwise, it is neither the letters of these names, nor the meanings that we conceive from them in our minds, which act in the universe.

God has promised to respond to the prayer of anyone who calls Him: I answer the supplicant’s call when he calls Me (2:186). As we said in our exposition of the verse,1 this promise implies two conditions: (1) It must be a true prayer. (2) It must be requested from God alone. If one breaks off from all apparent means and instruments, and instead connects to their Lord for any wish that they may have, then they have indeed connected to the reality of the divine name which would be relevant in the case of their request. Thus that name will function through its existential reality and respond to the person’s request. This is what is meant by “praying to God through His names.” Now, the extent to which one’s prayer is granted depends on the breadth of the name to which one connects. If one resorts to the Greatest Name, the person will enjoy an unconditional fulfillment of their prayer, because all things are subservient to the reality of the Greatest Name. This is how we should interpret the narrations and supplications in this regard, as opposed to the verbal or mental aspect of the names. When it is said [in some narrations] that God taught some of His names—or His Greatest Name—to one of His prophets or servants, it means that He opened the way for that servant to totally cut offthemselves from everything and turn wholeheartedly to God through calling Him with that name. This could be accompanied by some verbal utterance or mental concept, but that utterance or conception is meant as a shell to preserve those existential realities [of the person’s total detachment, and/ or the effects of the Greatest Name]. The letters and meanings are rather means and instruments in one way or another [not the reality of the Greatest Name]. The reader should reflect on this.

7. Are the Divine Names Reserved?

Based on our above discussions, it should be clear that there is no evidence for the reservation of the names (tawqifiyyat al-asmāʾ).1 Instead, we

have evidence against it. Some have drawn on the current verse—To Allah belong the most excellent names (al-asmāʾ al-ḥusná), so supplicate Him by them, and abandon those who commit sacrilege in His names (7:180)—to argue that the divine names are reserved [to what is found in the Qur’an and hadith]. This argument hinges on two conditions: (1) It assumes the article al- (“the” in the most excellent names) to be definite article, indicating what is already known and introduced (ʿahd). (2) It assumes that

“committing sacrilege in the divine names” means going beyond what is strictly found in scriptural sources. Both of these conditions can be disputed, as we explained above.2

They have also drawn on mustafīḍah (multiple, diffused, numerous)

narrations which effectively say: “Indeed there are 99 names for God—one less than 100. Whoever enumerates them shall enter paradise.” However, this does not prove the reservation and restriction of the divine names [to only what is transmitted through scriptural sources].

us to not name God with what is not found in the scriptural sources. With respect to the latter, permissible descriptions certainly go beyond that.

“God has created a name that is not pronounced through letters…” The descriptions given at the beginning of this hadith explicitly show that what is meant by “name” here is not a word, nor the mental concept indicated by the word. It should be clear that neither a word, nor the mental concept corresponding to it, has the features described in this hadith. Similarly, the next part of the hadith is not compatible with the common notion of a “name” [as a word or a mental concept]. Even if there is some word involved, what is meant by “name” here can only be an external entity that is designated by the word. In particular, when we take into account its three-fold elements of Allāh, Tabāraka and Taʿālá, we realize that this sense of the “name” cannot be anything but the divine essence—or something that subsists by the divine essence, and is certainly not external to it.

“God has created a name.” Given the above explanation, what is meant here is not what is commonly understood by “creation.” Rather, it means a certain appearance or manifestation of the divine essence, such that a particular name emerges from it. This confirms what we said previously: that there is a hierarchy within the divine names. Some of them are causes with respect to others; they act as a channel for the appearance and existence of their subordinate names. The chain extends all the way up, to

a name whose particular determination is a total lack of determination. The qualification of the divine essence by that name is tantamount to an absolute unconditionality.

“The manifest names are Allāh, Tabāraka and Taʿālá.” Here the hadith is describing general aspects which are a point of reference for all

particular aspects of perfection. Every need and lack in the world of creation is fulfilled by these three aspects of the divine: (1) Allāh: this name

indicates the divine essence in its most inclusive sense, as a collection of all perfections. (2) Tabāraka: this name indicates an affirmative aspect of the divine. It affirms every quality of perfection for it, and presents it as a source of every good and blessing. (3) Taʿālá: this name indicates a negational aspect of the divine. It negates all deficiency from it, and presents

“As actions that are attributable to that [pillar].” The demonstrative pronoun “that” here refers to the [three manifest] names. This is effectively what we said above: there is a causal hierarchy between the names, such that one emanates from another. The explicit mention of number 360 in this hadith proves that the divine names are not limited to 99.

“The three names are the pillars, while He has veiled the one [fourth] name.” The one which is “concealed and reserved” is still a “name,” which means that it is an expression and determination of the transcendent essence of God. At the same time, it is concealed and unmanifest by the virtue of its very nature and reality. This means that its expression lies in being unexpressed; its determination is lack of determination.1 This is what is meant by the idea that God is not delimited by any definition, including this very negational definition. He does not fall into any description or attribute, including this very negational description. The reason is

that these expressions are descriptions from us, while the divine essence is greater and higher than all our descriptions.

This means that the name Allāh—which embraces all divine qualities of perfections—is a reality that is inferior to the divine essence. It is also inferior to the concealed and reserved name of God. The same goes with Tabāraka and Taʿālá. These three names together veil and guard the concealed name, without any of them being higher than others. Then the four

of them—the three names, as well as the concealed name—are inferior to the divine essence. The divine essence, however, cannot be indicated by any expression or hint. That is because any phrase or sign that one may devise would serve as a “name,” which means that it is delimited [by the particular definition and determination of that name], while the divine essence is greater than and superior to any definition.

The hadith then refers to the verse: Say: Invoke “Allah” or invoke “the All-Merciful” (al-Raḥmān) That (ayyan) which you invoke, to Him belong (lahu) the most excellent names (17:110). The relevance of this verse to the hadith is that the pronoun in lahu (Him or It) refers to the word ayyan (that), and ayyan is a conditional noun (ism al-sharṭ) which indicates an indeterminate meaning. Its determinate meaning is lack of determination. It should also be evident that what is meant in this verse by Allāh and

They are “names” not in the linguistic sense, but in the sense that they denote God’s essence from the angle of a particular quality.
